title: Cthulhu Death May Die: 2026 Revisit and a Look at Season 4 (review)
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ATXZbbUsHVw

Daniel (@dungeondive) returns to *Cthulhu: Death May Die* after a long absence — a retail copy of Season 4 was the prompt — and uses the visit to re-argue why the game works.

The pitch is structural: it drops you into act three. Investigation, slow burn and mystery all happened offscreen; you arrive in media res with a ritual already underway and a couple of hours to break it. The sanity economy follows from that framing. Taking stress levels your investigator up, making them deadlier as they come apart, until one step too far kills them — a built-in timer that reads as character rather than bookkeeping. He also singles out the discovery decks (thirteen multi-use cards per episode, each folding event, test and reward into one) and the dice pool, where black dice carry tentacles that cost sanity while green bonus dice carry none.

Season 4 adds six episodes, six investigators, optional "unknown monster" groups offset by upgradeable relics, and four new insanities. Played here: Pyramid of Fear, a Raiders-flavoured crawl of exploration tokens, traps and a three-piece staff of Ra, run against Nyarlathotep.

The complaints are physical rather than mechanical — the minis and the enormous boxes they demand, the playmats he refuses to unfold on a small table, tiles he would trade for boards. He would rebuy the lot in standees tomorrow. And the final confrontation still devolves into a dice fest, as it does in *Arkham* and *Eldritch*.

----

Is shelf space a fair criterion for culling a game you genuinely enjoy — or is that judging the box rather than the game?
